title: How did Christianity go from persecuted to official?
subtitle: From Constantine to Theodosius
subject: histoire
description: In 313, Constantine granted Christians the right to practice their faith. In 380, Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire: in between came a council, endless quarrels and an emperor who tried to bring back the old gods.
author: vedran-obucina

hero.hook: In under seventy years, a barely tolerated religion became the only official faith of the Roman Empire.

blocks.text: In **312**, [[Constantine]] crushed his rival Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, at the gates of Rome. Now master of the Roman West, he began to support the Christians. The following year, with his fellow emperor Licinius, he issued the [[Edict of Milan]]: freedom of worship for Christians, and the return of the property confiscated from the churches during the persecutions.

The text made Christianity a lawful religion, not the official religion of the empire. The traditional cults remained permitted. Constantine funded churches and promoted Christians, but he left the old gods alone. How did this merely tolerated religion become, in under seventy years, the only faith recognized by the state?

sections.title: Constantine and the Council of Nicaea

blocks.text: The emperor's support changed the place of Christianity in Roman society. The churches received money and land. Their leaders, the bishops, now had access to the emperor and a say in his policies. Constantine also stepped into the quarrels among Christians. In **325**, he convened the [[Council of Nicaea]], an assembly of bishops asked to settle a burning question: who is Jesus, and what is his relationship to God the Father?

blocks.caption: The Council of Nicaea in a Byzantine fresco: Constantine enthroned among the bishops.

blocks.text: The council adopted the Nicene Creed, still at the heart of Christian belief today. But the emperor's presence did not bring unity. The followers of [[Arius]], a priest who refused to place Jesus on the same level as the Father, did not give up, and the quarrels went on for decades. The real change was political: Christianity had gained access to imperial power, its money and its institutions.

Constantine's successors did not all follow the same line. Some backed the Christians loyal to Nicaea, others favored rival currents, such as the Arians, whom their opponents considered heretics. Meanwhile, the rites of [[paganism]] were alive and well in the cities, in the countryside and above all in the army.

blocks.caption: The emperor Julian as a bearded philosopher: a statue kept in the Louvre.

blocks.text: In **361**, one emperor even tried to turn back the clock. [[Julian the Apostate]], raised a Christian but won over to the old gods, restored the traditional religion of Rome. He honored the ancient deities and cut off imperial funding to Christian institutions. His reign ended as early as **363**, but it proved one thing: Christianity had not simply replaced the old religious system. After him, Christian emperors returned to power. The law was moving faster than belief, and Roman society remained a mosaic of religions.

sections.title: Theodosius imposes the faith of Nicaea

blocks.text: In **380**, the emperor Theodosius I issued the [[Edict of Thessalonica]], together with Gratian and Valentinian II, who ruled the West. The text reserved the support of the state for Nicene Christianity alone, the faith that confesses the Trinity: one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

blocks.caption: The Missorium of Theodosius, a silver dish from 388: the emperor enthroned between Valentinian II and Arcadius.

blocks.text: This went much further than the law of 313. Constantine had given Christians freedom; Theodosius chose which form of Christianity the state recognized and tied it to imperial power. In the following decades, the authorities gradually restricted pagan worship and the Christian teachings that departed from Nicaea.

That does not mean that every inhabitant of the empire became Christian overnight. Many people went on honoring the old deities, and the rival Christian factions kept up their disputes. Religious life changed slowly, but it changed deeply and for good.

sections.title: A society changed to its core

blocks.text: Christianity now had recognized institutions, legal privileges and a lasting influence on public life. Bishops became key figures: they settled disputes, took part in the administration of the empire and served as diplomats. The Christian calendar spread: Sunday and the great feasts set the rhythm of public life. Roman law, and later European law, developed in societies where Christian ideas shaped marriage, family, sexuality and religious practice.

Between the legalization of 313 and the edict of 380, fewer than **70 years** went by. For the legal status of Christianity, it was an upheaval. But the deepest transformation took centuries. The emperor had changed the law; he could not change overnight the way people believed, lived and thought.

Constantine legalized Christianity, but he was not baptized until near the end of his life. Becoming the political patron of the Christians and becoming a fully initiated Christian were not necessarily one and the same moment.
Constantine made Christianity legal in 313 and Theodosius made it the official religion in 380: the law flipped within two generations, while belief took centuries to follow.
